Round 1's central finding -- AC-001 and AC-009 verifying less than their parent requirements demanded -- is genuinely closed, not merely narrated: AC-001 (requirements.md:31-35) requires 'all three elements... not merely the mode name, and not merely the exit code' and TEST-001 (acceptance-tests.md:27) repeats the same non-heading, non-exit-code-only exclusion; AC-009 (requirements.md:97-103) requires 'two assertions, both required' and TEST-009 (acceptance-tests.md:75-79) mirrors it. The new AC-013/TEST-013 (requirements.md:83-89, acceptance-tests.md:89-93) requires both server-name presence and a stated trust posture, so it does not reproduce the single-assertion defect it was added to avoid. Minor, non-blocking observation: TEST-003's prose (acceptance-tests.md:37-38) lists 7 sub-cases (unset, empty, 600, 1, 0, -5, abc) but describes only 'first three... last three' (6), leaving the value 1 unclassified by that summary sentence; AC-003's own text ('rejects a non-numeric or non-positive value') and AC-004's reuse of TIMEOUT=1 as the standard valid bound make 1's classification unambiguous in practice, so this does not block a downstream test author's decision.

Non-goals (requirements.md:121-128) explicitly excludes retries, rewriting the already-correct absent/error path, adding new output-validation code, re-documenting the Codex agent-role surface, changing check-cross-model's logic, and pinning/vendoring vendor CLIs -- each with a stated reason. Baseline Constraints (requirements.md:146-152) reinforce the same boundaries (BL-001 through BL-005). No requirement or AC implies unbounded expansion beyond these stated limits.

Baseline Constraints BL-001 through BL-005 (requirements.md:148-152) state behaviour-preservation for the absent/error path, an unchanged check-cross-model, extension-not-replacement of existing policy text, mandatory dual-runtime parity, and a guard-protection boundary verified directly against guard-invariants.generated.js:5 (INV-017, cited requirements.md:152). The Assumptions section (requirements.md:142-144) states the SIGTERM/SIGKILL escalation constraint explicitly and requires it be exercised by a test (Edge Case 7, TEST-004(b)) rather than left assumed.

The behaviour-changing claim (hung panelist now fails the gate) has a concrete validation surface: AC-005/AC-006 and TEST-005/TEST-006 (acceptance-tests.md:59-67), composed against the real check-cross-model gate. The corrected malformed-output exit-code claim (requirements.md:27-29, citing run-panelist-gpt.sh:241-297) is a second high-risk claim -- it reverses this specification's own prior error (exit 2 -> exit 1) -- but that file is outside this review's allowed manifest and I could not verify it directly. Noting this plainly rather than assuming either way: its validation surface is the Assumptions section's 're-verify every file:line... at implementation start' instruction (requirements.md:144) plus the explicit Non-goal against writing new validation code for this path (requirements.md:125); no acceptance test independently re-derives the exit code from the runner script itself (TEST-001 is a policy-document read, not a runner-script execution), so if the citation is wrong, detection is deferred to that named re-verification step rather than caught by this feature's own test suite. That is a named, if thinner-than-executable, validation surface, which is what this check requires.
